o: Count triples i<j<k with (nums[i]+nums[j]+nums[k]) % d == 0. Only remainders mod d matter. A clean O(n²) technique fixes the middle index j: keep a hash map of remainders of all i < j, and for each k > j add the count of the complementary remainder (−nums[j]−nums[k]) mod d.
k: Work modulo d: only nums[i] % d affects divisibility.
Fixing the middle element lets a running 'left remainders' map answer all (i,k) pairs around it in O(1) each.
Complement lookup: needed remainder r satisfies r + a + b ≡ 0 (mod d), i.e. r = (−a−b) mod d.

a.n: Middle-element sweep with a remainder map
a.i: Iterate j from 0 to n−1. Before processing j as middle, the map holds remainders of indices < j. For every k > j, query the map for (−nums[j]−nums[k]) mod d and add to the answer. After all k for this j, insert nums[j]'s remainder into the map.
s: Initialize an empty counter of remainders.
For each j, first loop k from j+1 to n−1 adding counter[(−nums[j]−nums[k]) mod d].
a.t: O(n²) — for each middle j we scan all k > j with O(1) map lookups.
a.sp: O(min(n, d)) — the remainder counter holds at most n distinct keys.

w: Beware negative-modulo behavior in C++/Java/JS: normalize with ((x % d) + d) % d. An alternative O(u²) approach counts remainder frequencies and enumerates remainder triples with binomial coefficients — worth mentioning if n were much larger. Triplet count can exceed 32-bit? n = 1000 gives at most ~1.6e8 triples, safe in int but use long defensively. Follow-up: quadruples, or count triples with sum ≡ r for arbitrary r.
